title: Given the root of a binary tree and two nodes, find their lowest common ancestor, which is the deepest node that has both target nodes as descendants.
shortTitle: Lowest Common Ancestor: recursive: if left and right both non-null, current is LCA
keyPoints: LCA is the deepest node whose subtree contains both target nodes as descendants
A single post-order traversal answers the question without storing explicit paths
If both children return non-null, the current node is the LCA; otherwise propagate the non-null result
The base case returns the node itself if it is null or equals either target
Time is O(n) visiting each node once; space is O(h) for the recursion stack
For a BST, use the ordering property to walk down in O(h) time instead of this general algorithm

s1_definition.oneliner: Recurse both sides; if each side finds one target, the current node is the lowest common ancestor, otherwise pass up whichever side found something.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)** is the deepest node whose subtree contains both target nodes.
- **Post-order recursion** searches the tree once, with each call returning a signal about what it found.
- **Base case** returns the node itself if it is null or if it equals either target.
- **Split rule** says if both left and right return non-null, the current node is the LCA.
- **Propagation** passes up the non-null result when only one side found a target.
- **Time** is O(n); **space** is O(h) for the call stack.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh and Priya work in different teams of the National Bank of India, and HR wants to find the lowest-level manager who oversees both of them. Starting from the top, each manager asks: is either person found in my left team, my right team, or am I one of them? If one target is found on the left and the other on the right, this manager is the lowest common boss. If both are found on the same side, the answer lies deeper on that side.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Post-order LCA traversal
  =========================

  Tree:        3
              / \
             5    1
            / \  / \
           6   2 0   8
              / \
             7   4

  LCA(5, 1):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  At 3: search left, search right│
  │    At 5: root==p → return 5     │
  │    At 1: root==q → return 1     │
  │  left=5, right=1                │
  │  Both non-null → return 3 (LCA)│
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  Decision at each node:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ null or target? → return node      │
  │ left = recurse(left)               │
  │ right = recurse(right)             │
  │ both non-null?  → return this (LCA)│
  │ else → return whichever is non-null│
  └────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Lowest Common Ancestor of two nodes is the deepest node whose subtree contains both of them. The recursive solution is elegant because a single post-order traversal answers it without storing explicit paths. Each recursive call returns a node that signals what its subtree found. The base case returns the current node if it is null or if it is one of the two targets.

For an internal node, you recurse into both children and then decide based on what they report. If both return non-null, one target was found in each subtree, so the current node is the LCA. If only one side returns non-null, both targets live in that subtree, so you propagate that result upward. This clean three-way decision is the whole algorithm.

The time is O(n) and the space is O(h). For a BST, the ordering property lets you walk down from the root in O(h) time, going left when both targets are smaller and right when both are larger, with the split point being the LCA. Always mention the assumption that both targets exist; if one might be absent, use a stricter variant that confirms both were found.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in a conflict-of-interest check. The approval hierarchy is a tree, and for two employees involved in the same transaction the system finds the lowest-level manager who oversees both, because that manager is accountable for the conflict.

Remember one sentence: if both children return a target, the current node is the LCA; if only one does, propagate it up.
